title: Which Transformation Initiative Should Be Funded, and How Will Success Be Established?
tagline: ChangeWorks: a transformation portfolio laboratory where every benefit keeps its class. Cash, avoided cost, revenue and released capacity are never summed into one number without a declared conversion; the approved baseline is immutable and a forecast revision never overwrites it; adoption ramps and benefit lags are modelled rather than assumed; two initiatives claiming the same capacity are counted once and the residual is explained before a scenario can be proposed; and nothing in the product funds anything. The known answer: a cost of 1,000 at period 0 and inflows of 600 in periods 1 and 2 at a 10% annual rate give an NPV of 5000/121 = 41.32, with simple and discounted payback labelled separately and 800 capacity hours kept out of the cash flow. Synthetic data; project 09 of the Business Data Lab.
kind: Dashboard · Transformation · Business case · FastAPI · React
tech: Python 3.11 (exact rationals for discount factors and ratios, decimals for money; no floating point in a published figure)
PostgreSQL 16 (immutable approved baselines, append-only assumption and forecast versions, NUMERIC(20,6) money)
FastAPI 0.162 (commands with idempotency keys, 401/403/409/422 contracts; a scenario can be proposed, never funded)
SQL reference recomputation of every metric
GitHub Actions (postgres:16 service, hosted runners only)
399 Python tests, 2,431 TypeScript golden and snapshot checks plus 63 review checks over 34 worlds, 80 browser tests
note: Everything is synthetic: the 24 initiatives, 30 baselines, 900 cost items, 700 benefit items, 30 scenarios, 144 forecast rows and every figure come from a seeded generator whose designed relationships and twelve injected defects are published in an injection manifest, together with the choices its author made after seeing earlier draws (a discovery cost added in period 0 to every initiative, benefit shares normalised, one volume floor, extra observation readings, the adoption-ramp range, one performance level and one revision date moved); benefits are recognised for twelve periods per stream, so the published NPVs and paybacks describe a first-year case and the site says so. The public site is a static demo over a published snapshot; the sensitivity lab, roadmap edits and scenario selection simulate their actions in browser memory, and nothing is proposed, revised or funded from them. The transactional behaviour (establishing and approving a baseline, assessing an opportunity, building cash flows, mapping impacts, assessing readiness, planning the roadmap, proposing a scenario, recording adoption, tracking benefits, revising a forecast) is verified separately on GitHub-hosted runners against a transient PostgreSQL. Built from a written specification by a coordinating session delegating bounded work to implementation subagents; not a measurement of any real organisation.
problem:
The transformation portfolio review argues about a spreadsheet. Time savings are booked as cash savings although nobody's hours were removed from payroll; two initiatives claim the same released capacity; an annual discount rate was applied to monthly periods; benefits start before the system is deployed; training completion is reported as adoption; the forecast was overwritten after a missed target so the original approval is gone; a dependency loop makes the roadmap impossible; a one-time licence recurs every month by accident; and avoided cost is added to realised savings as if both were cash.

ChangeWorks fixes the arithmetic first: four benefit classes kept apart, a cash flow that admits capacity only through a declared conversion, a discount rate whose basis matches the period, benefits that cannot precede deployment, adoption with its denominator preserved and training kept separate, an immutable approved baseline with every forecast revision beside it, a dependency graph that refuses cycles and reports shared-resource conflicts, a double-count residual that must be explained, and a scenario whose only reachable state is proposed.
built:
Two implementations of one contract, checked against a hand calculation and each other.

  • The contract: benefit classes cash, avoided cost, revenue and capacity with amounts in money or hours; net cash flow from the cash classes only, avoided cost entering only with evidence of realisation and capacity only through a conversion assumption that names its hourly rate and staffing evidence; one-time costs in exactly one period and recurring costs expanded over a half-open range; NPV as an exact rational over the declared rate whose basis must equal the period basis, with an annual rate on monthly periods converted explicitly and recorded; simple and discounted payback as the first period whose cumulative flow reaches zero, each with an interpolated figure and null when never crossed; benefits that cannot start before deployment and ramps that keep the unramped plan visible; capacity released as volume times minutes saved over sixty; an approved baseline that only a new version can correct; forecast revisions that never overwrite the original; cost variance and benefit realisation within one benefit type on matured periods with the baseline trend shown beside the raw change; dependency delay from feasible starts with cycles refused and resource overallocation reported apart; readiness as a weighted assessment, not a probability; a double-count residual counted once per shared source key; and a proposal that is never a funding.
  • A known-answer fixture written first: the 1,000 then 600 and 600 case at 10% gives NPV 5000/121 = 41.32, simple payback in period 2 (1.6667 interpolated) and discounted payback in period 2 (1.9167), with 800 capacity hours excluded and 400.0000 hours of capacity released; a second initiative with recurring costs, a ramp and an avoided-cost benefit whose NPV is −57.85; a third that never pays back (both paybacks null, not rejected); a dependency chain with delays of 2 and 3 periods; two initiatives sharing one cost line, giving a double-count residual of 75.00 explained by that key; readiness, adoption, training, risk exposure, cost variance and a forecast revised once with the original kept; plus a rejected variant (30 rejected records on monthly periods: a repeated one-time cost, an annual rate on monthly periods, a benefit before deployment, a dependency cycle, an overallocated resource, a capacity benefit claiming cash without a conversion) and an empty variant. A standard-library script reproduces all 1,810 checks from the records.
  • The Python domain, PostgreSQL schema and FastAPI commands: establish and approve a baseline, assess an opportunity, build cash flows, map impacts, assess readiness, plan the roadmap, select a scenario as proposed, record adoption, track benefits and revise a forecast; 346 tests on a GitHub-hosted runner against PostgreSQL 16 including the twelve adversarial scenarios of the specification detected and recovered, and an independent SQL recomputation that agrees with the domain on the fixtures, at fourteen other instants and on sixty seeded populations.
  • The static site: the same contract in TypeScript with rational arithmetic only, a portfolio overview with benefits by class and the double-count residual, baseline evidence, the business case with its assumption versions, a sensitivity lab, the roadmap with dependencies and resource lanes, change impact, readiness review, the benefits register, forecast comparison, evidence and the case study; 2,431 golden and snapshot checks against the Python domain at five instants, six windows, seven horizons and a 61-point rate grid, 63 review-finding checks over 34 hand-worked worlds, and 80 Playwright tests at four widths and 200% zoom.
  • A deterministic synthetic world: 24 initiatives in four programmes over 36 monthly periods, 30 process baselines in two approved versions, 160 assumption versions, 900 cost and 700 benefit items across the four classes with ramps and lags, 40 dependencies, 8 shared resources, 60 stakeholder groups, 300 readiness assessments, 500 adoption observations, 200 training completions, 400 benefit observations with baseline trends, 120 risks, 30 scenarios and 12 forecast version sets, with seven designed relationships and twelve injected defects (time savings booked as cash, two initiatives claiming one capacity, an annual rate applied monthly, a benefit before deployment, training read as adoption, a forecast overwrite, a dependency cycle, a never-paying-back case shown with a payback, an overallocated specialist, an improvement attributed entirely to the rollout, a one-time cost recurring, avoided cost added to cash) published with how each must be handled.

steps.title: The known answer before any volume
steps.body: A cost of 1,000 at period 0, inflows of 600 in periods 1 and 2, a 10% annual rate: NPV is −1000 + 600/1.1 + 600/1.21 = 5000/121 = 41.32. The undiscounted cumulative flow reaches zero in period 2 (1.6667 interpolated) and the discounted one in period 2 (1.9167); both are labelled. The 800 capacity hours on the same initiative stay out of the cash flow because no conversion assumption exists. A standard-library script reproduces every figure from the records before the application exists.

steps.title: Four classes, one conversion rule
steps.body: Cash and revenue enter the cash flow. Avoided cost enters only with evidence that a budget line was removed; otherwise it is shown beside the flow. Capacity enters only as a derived cash item that cites an hourly rate and staffing evidence; hours are never a payroll saving by themselves.

steps.title: Nothing is overwritten, nothing is funded
steps.body: An approved baseline is frozen; a correction is a new version with a reason. A forecast revision creates the next version and the comparison shows the original, every revision and the observed values. Selecting a scenario makes it proposed; the product has no funded state.

steps.title: Two modes, disclosed
steps.body: Mode A is the backend on a GitHub-hosted runner with a transient PostgreSQL. Mode B is the public site over a published snapshot; the sensitivity lab, roadmap edits and scenario selection simulate their actions in browser memory, and nothing is proposed or revised from them.

results:
The business case on the synthetic snapshot (scenario scn-025, the one carrying the designed relationships; the cash-flow table carries the assumption version beside each row):

The portfolio overview on a phone:

What the data supports. In the scenario that carries the designed relationships, the 24 initiatives plan costs of 25,914,200.00 against cash benefits of 15,288,067.20, revenue of 6,074,000.13, evidenced avoided cost of 5,516,433.35 and converted capacity of 1,774,010.55, with a further 4,025,383.47 of avoided cost shown beside the cash flow and 145,045.60 capacity hours not converted; the portfolio NPV is 1,438,382.25 over the first-year case, six initiatives never reach simple payback and six never reach discounted payback. Two initiatives claim the same finance team's capacity, so planned benefits of 32,677,894.70 count 32,470,748.38 once and the residual of 207,146.32 must be explained before the scenario can be proposed. One initiative's only benefit is released capacity: 2,920.49 hours that never enter the cash flow without a conversion, an NPV of −761,535.73 and no payback. One initiative returns 0.620043 of its cost and never pays back; the page shows null, not a date. One forecast was revised twice after observed periods fell more than ten percent short, from 745,800.06 to 598,900.05 to 534,207.54, with the original kept beside the revisions. A shared specialist is at capacity in three periods and three further requests were refused. Across the portfolio adoption reaches half of the eligible population four to six periods after training reaches ninety percent (training completion 0.888443 against adoption 0.532881), and one initiative's observed improvement is 0.848744 baseline trend, shown beside the raw change as observed, not attributed. These are the generator's designed relationships and the one-draw realisation, published in its manifest and found by the site; they are not findings about any real organisation.

Found during the build. The generator's author found that the payback rule lets a cumulative flow of exactly zero at period 0 count as paid back, so an initiative whose first flow comes later would show a payback of zero; the world carries a planned discovery cost in period 0 for every initiative, the evidence page states the rule, and the rule changes in the fix round. An independent review of the published site has not run yet; its findings will be added here.

Not built yet: resource levelling that shifts starts, a database-level guard on the proposal rule, and the partial-trend-coverage warning.
